cards.title: Trump-Xi Beijing Summit Signals a Bargain Over Trade, Taiwan, and Iran
cards.background: US President Donald Trump concluded a two-day summit in Beijing with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on 15 May 2026. The visit was framed as an attempt to reset US-China relations, with the two sides discussing trade, Taiwan, and the war on Iran. The article does not provide a detailed readout of any agreement, but the summit itself signals direct leader-level bargaining on the core flashpoints in the bilateral relationship.

prop_args.thesis: Leader-level engagement between the US and China can reduce escalation risk by creating a direct channel for bargaining on trade, Taiwan, and Iran.
mechanisms: First, summit diplomacy lowers miscalculation. This is because (1) direct leader-to-leader contact reduces the chance that ambiguous military or economic signals are interpreted as hostile intent, (2) it allows both sides to clarify red lines on Taiwan and Iran without public posturing, and (3) it creates a personal commitment mechanism that bureaucracies can use to slow down escalation.

Second, a reset on trade can stabilize the wider relationship. Three reasons: one, trade interdependence gives both sides a material incentive to avoid tariff spirals and export controls; two, even partial deals can restore business confidence and reduce supply-chain uncertainty; three, economic cooperation can spill over into broader crisis management by making confrontation costlier.

Third, bargaining over Taiwan and Iran can produce managed competition rather than open conflict. This matters because (1) if the US and China can tacitly coordinate on restraint, Taiwan becomes less likely to become a trigger for immediate military escalation, (2) China may be more willing to pressure Iran if it gets concessions elsewhere, and (3) even limited understandings can buy time for de-escalation in multiple theaters simultaneously.

opp_args.thesis: The summit is more likely to entrench great-power bargaining and strategic ambiguity, which increases pressure on smaller states and makes flashpoints like Taiwan and Iran more dangerous.
mechanisms: First, bilateral summitry can normalize sphere-of-influence politics. One, if the US and China negotiate over Taiwan as a bargaining chip, it signals that smaller states' security can be traded for great-power stability; two, this weakens deterrence because allies and partners cannot be sure the US will defend them consistently; three, it encourages China to keep probing for concessions through coercion rather than compromise.

Second, trade talks may be used as leverage rather than genuine liberalization. One, both sides can weaponize market access, tariffs, and export controls to extract political concessions; two, this creates a cycle where economic interdependence becomes a tool of coercion instead of peace; three, firms and third countries face higher uncertainty because any deal can be reversed in the next crisis.

Third, discussing Iran in a US-China summit risks transactional side deals that worsen regional instability. One, China may reduce pressure on Iran only if it gets benefits on trade or Taiwan, which incentivizes opportunistic behavior; two, Iran can interpret great-power bargaining as cover to escalate or delay compromise; three, Middle Eastern security becomes dependent on US-China relations rather than on durable regional deterrence or diplomacy.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether summit diplomacy creates credible restraint or merely formalizes great-power bargaining. Prop wins if you think direct communication meaningfully reduces miscalculation; opp wins if you think the real effect is to legitimize coercive trade-offs over Taiwan and Iran, with smaller states bearing the downside.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue leader-level summit diplomacy with China
THBT the US should prioritize direct bargaining with China over containment
THP a world where great powers negotiate over regional flashpoints through summit diplomacy

cards.title: US Cartel Prosecutions Turn Mexican Security Apparatus Into a Bilateral Flashpoint
cards.background: On May 11, 2026, US authorities arrested Gerardo Merida Sanchez, Mexico’s former public security secretary in Sinaloa state, in Arizona and later transferred him to New York. He was charged in a Manhattan federal indictment unsealed on April 29 alongside former Sinaloa governor Ruben Rocha, alleging they conspired with the Sinaloa Cartel to import narcotics into the US in exchange for political support and bribes. Prosecutors allege Merida Sanchez accepted more than $100,000 per month from Los Chapitos, used police to shield cartel operations, and leaked raid intelligence, including advance warning before at least 10 raids in 2023.

prop_args.thesis: US prosecution of cartel-linked Mexican officials is necessary to break the state-cartel nexus that makes anti-narcotics enforcement fail from the inside.
mechanisms: First, it attacks the cartel's institutional protection network. This is because (1) cartels do not just rely on violence, they rely on compromised police and governors to survive, (2) removing senior officials raises the cost of collusion for future elites, and (3) it disrupts the information pipeline that lets cartels evade raids and investigations.

Second, it restores deterrence inside Mexican security institutions. Three reasons: one, public indictments show that office does not equal immunity, two, the threat of extradition and US custody weakens the incentive to take cartel money, and three, it forces lower-level officers to choose between career survival and criminal loyalty.

Third, it improves bilateral enforcement capacity. This matters because the US can use financial intelligence, extradition leverage, and cross-border prosecutions to reach actors that local institutions may be unable or unwilling to touch, making the crackdown more credible than purely domestic reform.

prop_args.thesis: Treating cartel-linked officials as transnational criminal targets strengthens rule of law and signals that political office cannot be used as a shield for organized crime.
mechanisms: First, it closes the impunity gap. One, local investigations can be blocked by captured prosecutors or governors, two, US federal courts provide an external venue when domestic accountability is compromised, and three, the public nature of indictments creates reputational and political costs even before conviction.

Second, it deters future collusion by making the payoff structure worse. One, bribes become riskier when officials know foreign prosecutors can trace payments and communications, two, cartel protection becomes harder to sustain when senior figures are arrested abroad, and three, the threat of asset freezes and travel restrictions hits the personal incentives of elites.

Third, it can weaken cartel territorial control over time. One, if security chiefs cannot reliably warn or protect traffickers, raids become more effective, two, rival groups and informants gain confidence to cooperate with authorities, and three, cartels lose the state resources that help them monopolize violence.

opp_args.thesis: US extraterritorial cartel prosecutions can backfire by politicizing anti-drug policy, undermining Mexican sovereignty, and making cooperation with Washington less sustainable.
mechanisms: First, they trigger nationalist backlash inside Mexico. One, when US prosecutors indict governors and security chiefs, Mexican leaders can frame it as foreign interference, two, that framing protects accused officials politically even if evidence exists, and three, it makes the public less willing to trust US claims or cooperate with joint operations.

Second, they can degrade intelligence-sharing. One, Mexican officials become more cautious about sharing sensitive information if they fear it will be used in US indictments, two, agencies may compartmentalize or slow cooperation to protect domestic political allies, and three, the result is fewer joint operations and weaker operational access to cartels.

Third, they may incentivize securitized escalation over institution-building. One, designating cartels as 'terrorist organisations' and using terrorism statutes pushes the issue toward militarized enforcement, two, militarization often produces more violence and civilian harm without dismantling corruption, and three, it diverts attention from police reform, prosecution capacity, and anti-money-laundering work.

opp_args.thesis: Targeting individual officials is insufficient because cartel capture is systemic, so the arrests may produce headlines without changing the underlying political economy of organized crime.
mechanisms: First, the supply of corruptible officials remains. One, cartel profits are large enough to buy new collaborators, two, removing one security chief does not eliminate the incentives facing local police and politicians, and three, the network simply adapts by recruiting replacements.

Second, enforcement can be selectively symbolic. One, high-profile indictments are easier than dismantling financing and logistics chains, two, prosecutors may focus on politically useful cases rather than the most damaging nodes, and three, the cartel's core trafficking capacity can survive even if a few elites are exposed.

Third, the crackdown can fragment violence rather than reduce it. One, when a cartel loses state protection, rival groups compete for territory, two, splintering increases homicide and instability in the short term, and three, communities may experience worse insecurity even if the state claims progress.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether external prosecution actually changes cartel-state incentives or just provokes sovereignty backlash. Prop wins if you prioritize breaking entrenched impunity and the information shield around cartels; opp wins if you think the decisive constraint is political cooperation, which US indictments may undermine.

THBT the US should designate Mexican cartels as terrorist organisations
THP a world where foreign governments can indict and extradite officials for transnational organized crime
TH, as Mexico, would cooperate with US prosecutions of cartel-linked politicians and security officials

cards.title: U.S. Energy Blockade Turns Cuba Into a Coercive Bargaining Chip in a Regime-Change Push
cards.region: Cuba / United States / Caribbean / Latin America
cards.background: On May 15, 2026, CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Havana to deliver a message from President Donald Trump that the United States would only seriously engage on economic and security issues if Cuba made “fundamental changes.” The Trump administration has publicly framed Cuba as part of its broader “Donroe Doctrine,” while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington could not change Cuba’s trajectory while the current regime remains in power. The trip came hours after Havana said it had run out of fuel, with Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy reporting no fuel oil or diesel and blackouts in Havana exceeding 20-22 hours; Cuba says the crisis worsened after the U.S. seized Venezuelan oil assets and imposed a blockade barring foreign oil from reaching the island.

prop_args.thesis: The U.S. can use energy leverage to force political concessions from a vulnerable authoritarian regime, making coercive diplomacy more effective than indefinite containment.
mechanisms: First, the blockade creates immediate material pain that the Cuban state cannot easily absorb. This is because (1) Cuba has no fuel oil or diesel, (2) blackouts in Havana exceed 20-22 hours, and (3) the regime’s legitimacy depends on basic service delivery, so energy scarcity directly raises the domestic cost of defiance.

Second, tying aid to reforms gives Washington a credible bargaining chip rather than a blank check. Three reasons: one, the U.S. can condition $100 million in humanitarian aid on “meaningful reforms”; two, Cuba needs external relief to prevent collapse; three, selective relief lets the U.S. reward compliance while preserving pressure if Havana stalls.

Third, coercive pressure can weaken the regime’s external lifelines and reduce hostile great-power footholds. This matters because Cuba is accused by Washington of hosting Russian and Chinese intelligence activity, so forcing concessions could limit adversarial access 90 miles from Florida and improve U.S. regional security.

opp_args.thesis: The blockade and regime-change pressure will backfire by entrenching the Cuban government, worsening humanitarian suffering, and pushing Havana closer to rival powers.
mechanisms: First, external coercion lets the regime frame every hardship as U.S. aggression. One, Díaz-Canel can blame blackouts and shortages on a “genocidal energy blockade”; two, that narrative reduces domestic blame on the government; three, repression becomes easier when the state can present dissent as collaboration with a foreign enemy.

Second, sanctions-style pressure often strengthens authoritarian resilience rather than producing reform. One, the leadership can ration scarce resources to loyalists and security forces; two, the opposition suffers most from shortages and is less able to organize; three, the regime can survive longer than the population, meaning the policy extracts pain without achieving change.

Third, coercion increases dependency on China and Russia instead of reducing it. One, if the U.S. cuts off fuel and aid, Cuba has stronger incentives to seek alternative financing and intelligence support; two, that expands rival influence in the Caribbean; three, the U.S. ends up with a more isolated but not more democratic Cuba.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether pain translates into leverage or just suffering. The proposition wins if it proves the Cuban state is so dependent on external energy that the U.S. can trade relief for reforms; the opposition wins if it shows authoritarian regimes can absorb coercion, redirect blame, and survive while civilians bear the costs.

THBT states should prioritize coercive diplomacy over unconditional humanitarian aid when dealing with hostile authoritarian regimes
THP a world where major powers can condition energy access on political liberalization
TH, as a regional power, would trade relief for regime concessions in neighboring authoritarian states

cards.title: Trump’s Beijing Reset Exposes the Limits of MAGA China Hawkishness
cards.background: Donald Trump visited Beijing this week after years of campaigning on hardline anti-China rhetoric and after imposing tariffs that rose from 10% in February 2025 to 145% by mid-April. China retaliated with 125% tariffs and restrictions on rare earth exports, escalating the trade war. In Beijing, Trump praised Xi Jinping as a friend and touted unspecified trade deals, while key unresolved issues remained, especially Taiwan and a delayed $14bn US arms sale to the island. The Chinese read-out warned that failure to address Taiwan could lead to 'clashes and even conflicts,' while the White House statement omitted Taiwan entirely.

prop_args.thesis: Trump’s softer Beijing posture is a pragmatic correction that can reduce economic damage without meaningfully conceding core US interests.
mechanisms: First, de-escalation lowers the immediate costs of a tariff war. This is because (1) 145% US tariffs and 125% Chinese retaliation are already choking trade flows, (2) China’s rare earth export restrictions create supply-chain risk for US industry, and (3) even modest deals like Nvidia access, Boeing orders, and Citi approvals show that selective bargaining can recover value that blanket confrontation destroys.

Second, a top-down reset gives the US more leverage than performative hawkishness. Three reasons: one, Trump’s personal diplomacy can override bureaucratic inertia and force faster dealmaking; two, Beijing is more likely to respond to direct leader-level incentives than to diffuse congressional pressure; three, the administration can trade tone for concrete concessions on market access, IP, and sectoral openings without abandoning strategic competition.

Third, softening rhetoric can preserve room for long-term competition on the issues that actually matter. This matters because the US does not need constant escalation to contain China; it needs targeted pressure on technology, security, and supply chains, while avoiding a full economic rupture that hurts American consumers, firms, and allies more than it hurts Beijing.

opp_args.thesis: Trump’s Beijing reset signals weakness, emboldens China, and undermines the credibility of US deterrence on Taiwan and trade.
mechanisms: First, inconsistency destroys bargaining credibility. One, Trump spent years framing China as an existential economic enemy, so a sudden friendly pivot makes future threats less believable; two, Beijing learns that escalation can be rewarded with concessions and softer rhetoric; three, if the US backs away from the $14bn Taiwan arms sale, allies and adversaries will infer that Washington is willing to trade security commitments for short-term trade optics.

Second, the softening weakens the domestic coalition for sustained China containment. One, MAGA hawks like Steve Bannon and congressional China critics are already uneasy, which fractures the coalition needed for durable policy; two, if Trump’s base follows his tone, anti-China policy becomes personality-driven rather than institutionally anchored; three, that makes US policy volatile across administrations, encouraging China to wait out pressure rather than reform.

Third, the dealmaking approach risks strategic overreach and under-delivery. One, the article shows the concrete gains are modest and vague compared with the scale of the trade war; two, the core structural problems—market access, IP theft, subsidies—remain unresolved after eight years of tariffs; three, if the US normalizes symbolic summits without enforcement, China gets legitimacy and time while the US gets headlines instead of concessions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term economic stabilization and long-term strategic credibility. The prop side wins if the judge prioritizes avoiding self-harm from tariff escalation; the opp side wins if they frame Taiwan and deterrence as irreversible credibility goods that are far harder to rebuild once Trump signals softness.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue a softer diplomatic approach to China
THBT the United States should prioritize trade normalization over tariff escalation with China
THP a world where US-China relations are managed through leader-level bargaining rather than institutional confrontation

cards.title: Trump-China Trip Raises the Stakes Between Strategic De-Risking and Great-Power Bargaining
cards.background: Bloomberg's 'Balance of Power: Early Edition' on 15 May 2026 discussed the conclusion of President Trump's trip to China. The segment featured Bloomberg Washington correspondents Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz, alongside Republican Congressman Vince Fong, Stonecourt Capital Partner Rick Davis, Third Way Executive Vice President Jim Kessler, and former Fed Vice Chair Lael Brainard. The article itself is a short program listing and does not provide substantive policy details, agreements, or outcomes from the trip.

prop_args.thesis: A high-level Trump-China summit can reduce immediate escalation risk and create room for transactional deals that stabilize the bilateral relationship.
mechanisms: First, direct leader-to-leader diplomacy lowers the chance of miscalculation. This is because (1) it creates a clear channel for signaling red lines, (2) it reduces reliance on ambiguous bureaucratic messaging, and (3) it can quickly de-escalate crises before they spill into tariffs, sanctions, or military posturing.

Second, even limited transactional agreements can improve predictability for markets and firms. Three reasons: one, businesses can plan around clearer rules on tariffs, export controls, and investment screening; two, supply chains benefit from reduced policy shock; three, investors price in lower geopolitical risk, which supports trade and capital flows.

Third, summitry can buy time for longer-term strategic management. This matters because it allows both sides to compartmentalize disputes, preserve cooperation on issues like finance or fentanyl enforcement, and avoid a spiral where every disagreement becomes a zero-sum confrontation.

opp_args.thesis: A Trump-China trip is more likely to legitimize coercive bargaining and deepen strategic dependence without resolving the underlying rivalry.
mechanisms: First, summit diplomacy can reward China and the US for hardball tactics rather than cooperation. One, if concessions are extracted through threats, both sides learn that escalation pays; two, temporary deals are fragile because they are not backed by durable institutions; three, this encourages repeated crisis bargaining instead of stable rules.

Second, any apparent normalization can mask deeper decoupling and security competition. One, firms may still face export controls, investment restrictions, and sanctions uncertainty; two, allies may interpret bilateral dealmaking as abandonment and hedge away from US leadership; three, China can use the optics of engagement to buy time while continuing military and industrial buildup.

Third, the trip can intensify domestic political polarization in the US. One, critics may frame it as appeasement while hawks demand tougher measures; two, policy swings become more likely across administrations; three, that volatility itself is damaging because it makes long-term strategy toward China less credible.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether summit diplomacy actually changes state behavior or merely manages optics. Prop wins if the round centers on immediate crisis reduction and market stability; opp wins if the clash is about structural rivalry, because one trip cannot reverse the incentives driving US-China competition.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue summit diplomacy with China
THBT the US should prioritize transactional engagement over containment in its China policy
THP a world where major powers rely more on leader-level summits to manage rivalry

cards.title: Israel’s Targeted Killing Policy Risks Collapsing Gaza’s Fragile Ceasefire and Disarmament Track
cards.background: Israel said it killed Hamas commander Izz ad-Din al-Haddad in an air strike on Gaza City, describing him as one of the architects of the 7 October 2023 attack. The strike hit a residential building known as Al-Mu'taz, and eyewitnesses said a second strike hit a car fleeing the scene; Hamas has not confirmed or denied Haddad’s death. The attack came despite a ceasefire that took effect on 10 October 2025, and the BBC reports that Israel has carried out regular strikes in Gaza since then. US-led peace efforts have stalled, with talks on Hamas disarmament deadlocked and Hamas reactivating its police force while reasserting authority in Gaza.

prop_args.thesis: Israel’s continued targeted strikes are necessary enforcement that prevents Hamas from exploiting the ceasefire to rearm, reconstitute command, and evade disarmament.
mechanisms: First, decapitation strikes degrade Hamas’s operational capacity. This is because (1) commanders like Haddad sit at the intersection of planning, discipline, and battlefield coordination, (2) removing them creates short-term confusion in command-and-control, and (3) that confusion raises the cost of reconstituting military capability during a ceasefire window.

Second, the strikes create credible deterrence against ceasefire cheating. Three reasons: one, Hamas can no longer assume that signing a ceasefire guarantees immunity for senior operatives; two, Israel signals that participation in the October 7 attack remains a standing target set; three, this increases the expected cost of refusing disarmament or reactivating armed structures.

Third, this improves bargaining leverage in the disarmament track. This matters because if Hamas believes it can preserve armed leadership while waiting out diplomacy, it has no incentive to concede; sustained pressure forces it to choose between political survival and military preservation, which is the only way to make demilitarisation credible.

opp_args.thesis: Israel’s strikes undermine the ceasefire and make disarmament and reconstruction less likely by convincing Hamas and civilians that compliance does not buy safety.
mechanisms: First, the strikes destroy trust in the ceasefire architecture. One, if Israel keeps attacking after the truce begins, Hamas can frame disarmament as unilateral surrender; two, that weakens moderates who argue for compliance; three, it makes future enforcement mechanisms look like cover for continued military action.

Second, the strikes strengthen Hamas politically and operationally. One, civilian casualties and strikes on residential buildings create recruitment and legitimacy gains for Hamas; two, the group can present itself as the only actor resisting Israeli coercion; three, that makes rearmament and police reassertion more likely, not less.

Third, the strikes risk collapsing the broader peace process. One, the US-led second phase depends on transitional governance and demilitarisation; two, repeated violations make third-party mediation harder because guarantors lose credibility; three, once the process is seen as dead, both sides revert to maximalist military logic.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercion produces compliance or backlash. Pro wins if you believe Hamas only disarms under sustained military pressure; opp wins if you think ceasefire legitimacy and civilian trust are the scarce resources that make any political settlement possible, and those are being destroyed faster than Hamas’s military capacity.

THBT ceasefire agreements with non-state armed groups should permit continued strikes on senior militants
THP a world where peace agreements prioritize coercive disarmament over immediate territorial reconstruction

cards.title: US Taiwan Concessions Signal a Shift From Deterrence to Bargaining With Beijing
cards.background: The article discusses whether the US is reducing its support for Taiwan amid a broader thaw in US-China relations under Donald Trump. It says the White House suspended a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan ahead of Trump’s visit to Beijing, after Trump had already made concessions following his earlier meeting with Xi Jinping. China continues to claim Taiwan as its sovereign territory, and Xi described Taiwan as “the single most important issue” in relations with the US.

prop_args.thesis: Dialling down support for Taiwan is a dangerous concession that weakens deterrence, emboldens Beijing, and increases the risk of coercion or conflict.
mechanisms: First, it undermines deterrence credibility. This is because (1) Taiwan’s security depends on the US signaling that military support will be sustained, (2) suspending a $14 billion arms sale creates doubt about future commitments, and (3) Beijing can interpret ambiguity as permission to intensify military pressure, gray-zone operations, or blockade planning.

Second, it shifts the bargaining balance toward China. Three reasons: one, Taiwan becomes a bargaining chip in US-China trade or diplomatic negotiations; two, once Washington shows willingness to trade away security commitments, Beijing has incentives to demand more concessions on tariffs, technology, and regional influence; three, allies and partners in Asia read this as US retrenchment, which weakens the broader anti-coercion coalition.

Third, it raises the probability of miscalculation and crisis escalation. This matters because if China believes the US is less willing to defend Taiwan, it may act more aggressively around the island, while Taiwan may respond by accelerating asymmetric defense or political signaling, creating a more unstable security environment with less room for crisis management.

opp_args.thesis: Reducing support for Taiwan can be a pragmatic de-escalation strategy that lowers immediate conflict risk and preserves US flexibility in managing China.
mechanisms: First, it can reduce provocation and buy time for diplomacy. One, arms sales and high-profile support are seen by Beijing as violations of the One China framework; two, dialing them back can lower the temperature during sensitive US-China negotiations; three, that may prevent a spiral in which symbolic support triggers military escalation.

Second, it helps the US prioritize broader strategic interests. One, Washington has to manage trade, technology, and global security issues with China, not only Taiwan; two, a limited concession on arms sales may secure gains elsewhere, such as tariff relief or crisis communication channels; three, if Taiwan is not immediately under attack, preserving room for maneuver may be more valuable than maximal signaling.

Third, Taiwan is not abandoned, only recalibrated. One, the US can continue informal support, intelligence sharing, and deterrence through presence without every arms package; two, Taiwan’s own defense spending and asymmetric capabilities matter more than one sale; three, a more measured approach may encourage Taipei to take its own defense seriously instead of relying on automatic US backing.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the concession is read as credible deterrence failure or as controlled de-escalation. Prop wins if the round is about long-term security architecture and alliance credibility; opp wins if the judge prioritizes immediate crisis avoidance and strategic flexibility in US-China relations.
motion_areas: TH, as the US, would maintain unconditional military support for Taiwan
THBT the US should not trade Taiwan security commitments for concessions from China
THP a world where the US reduces arms sales to Taiwan in exchange for improved relations with Beijing

cards.title: US-Brokered Ceasefire Extension Freezes, But Does Not Resolve, the Israel-Hezbollah Border War
cards.background: Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 45-day extension of a shaky ceasefire after two days of talks in Washington DC, according to the US state department. The truce was originally announced by US President Donald Trump on 16 April, but Israel and Hezbollah have continued exchanging fire almost daily since then. Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli strikes killed 22 people, including eight children, on Wednesday alone, while Lebanon says more than 1 million people have been displaced and 2,896 people have been killed since the conflict escalated on 2 March. Israel says 18 soldiers and four civilians have been killed over the same period, and it says its operations aim to create a buffer zone in southern Lebanon to prevent future Hezbollah attacks.

prop_args.thesis: Extending the ceasefire is the least-bad option because it buys time for diplomacy, reduces immediate civilian harm, and creates a framework for separating military escalation from political negotiation.
mechanisms: First, the extension lowers the probability of immediate escalation. This is because (1) both sides have already shown they will keep firing absent a formal pause, (2) a time-bound extension creates a clear off-ramp from constant retaliation, and (3) even a fragile pause can interrupt the action-reaction cycle that turns border clashes into full-scale war.

Second, it creates space for structured bargaining instead of battlefield bargaining. Three reasons: one, the state department has already set a political track for June and a security track at the Pentagon on May 29, so there is now an institutional process; two, military delegations can negotiate border arrangements, verification, and deconfliction mechanisms that are impossible under active bombardment; three, diplomacy is more likely to produce enforceable commitments when both sides face costs from continued fighting.

Third, it reduces civilian casualties and displacement in the short term. This matters because (1) more than one million people have already been displaced in Lebanon, (2) southern Lebanon has been under constant bombardment with reports of children among the dead, and (3) even temporary pauses can allow humanitarian access, medical evacuation, and reconstruction planning, which are valuable regardless of whether a final settlement is reached.

opp_args.thesis: A repeated ceasefire extension entrenches instability because it rewards escalation, gives both sides time to rearm, and substitutes performative diplomacy for a durable settlement.
mechanisms: First, the extension can incentivize continued low-level violence rather than compliance. One, Israel and Hezbollah have kept trading fire even after the original truce, showing that neither side sees the ceasefire as binding; two, if violations carry no decisive cost, each side learns that limited attacks can be used to signal resolve without triggering a full response; three, this normalizes a permanent gray-zone conflict instead of ending it.

Second, it gives military actors time to consolidate gains and prepare for the next round. One, Israel says it is creating a buffer zone in southern Lebanon, so a pause may simply lock in territorial facts on the ground; two, Hezbollah can use the lull to reposition fighters, repair infrastructure, and replenish rockets and drones; three, when both sides rearm under cover of diplomacy, the next war is likely to be deadlier and harder to deter.

Third, the ceasefire can weaken Lebanon's sovereignty and internal political balance. One, the talks are being mediated and sequenced by the US, which means Lebanon's security agenda is being shaped externally; two, Hezbollah's dominance in the south means any deal that ignores domestic power-sharing will lack legitimacy and enforcement; three, if the state cannot protect civilians while foreign powers manage the border, public trust in Lebanese institutions erodes further.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the extension is treated as a bridge to a real settlement or as a way to freeze an unresolved war. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes immediate harm reduction and the value of creating negotiating space; opp wins if they show the pause merely institutionalizes a cycle of rearmament and future escalation. The structural advantage is slightly with prop on short-term humanitarian impact, but opp has strong comparative on long-run durability if the extension lacks enforcement.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize ceasefire extensions over immediate military victory in Lebanon
THBT negotiated ceasefires in asymmetric conflicts do more harm than good
THP a world where border conflicts are managed through repeated temporary ceasefires and phased negotiations

cards.title: Trump-Era ICE Detention Expansion Triggers Federalism Clash Over Local Infrastructure and Environmental Law
cards.background: Officials in Social Circle, Georgia have sued ICE and DHS in US district court for the Middle District of Georgia over plans to convert a warehouse at 1365 East Hightower Trail into a large immigration detention facility. The town says the project could hold up to 10,000 detainees and employ about 2,500 workers, while Social Circle itself has only about 5,000 residents across roughly 11 square miles. The complaint argues the federal agencies bought the property in February and moved ahead without completing required environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Administrative Procedure Act, and that the facility would overwhelm local water, sewer, and public services.

prop_args.thesis: Federal detention mega-centers imposed on small towns are a textbook case of central government overreach that externalizes massive costs onto unwilling local communities.
mechanisms: First, the project shifts the fiscal and infrastructural burden onto a town that did not consent to host it. This is because (1) Social Circle's population is about 5,000 while the facility could hold 10,000 detainees and employ 2,500 workers, (2) the town says its water and sewer network is already strained, and (3) federal agencies can capture the policy benefit of mass detention while local taxpayers absorb the service costs.

Second, bypassing robust environmental review creates predictable public-health and governance failures. Three reasons: one, NEPA-style assessments are designed to identify whether a site can physically handle a project before construction begins; two, without them, agencies can understate risks like sewage overflow, water shortages, and contamination; three, once the facility is built, the town is locked into a high-cost, hard-to-reverse infrastructure crisis.

Third, local resistance matters because detention policy depends on territorial legitimacy and operational cooperation. This matters because (1) towns can obstruct permitting, utilities, roads, and emergency response, (2) visible conflict turns detention expansion into a political liability that slows implementation nationwide, and (3) forcing compliance against local opposition fuels broader backlash against federal immigration enforcement.

opp_args.thesis: The federal government should be able to site detention infrastructure where it is operationally efficient, even if local governments object, because immigration enforcement is a national function.
mechanisms: First, centralized siting avoids a patchwork of local vetoes that would make immigration enforcement impossible. One, if every town can block facilities, the federal government cannot scale detention capacity at all; two, immigration control is constitutionally and politically a federal responsibility; three, allowing local lawsuits to stall projects creates a de facto sanctuary-by-zoning system.

Second, the town's harms may be manageable through mitigation, making the lawsuit an overreach rather than a necessity. One, federal agencies can upgrade utilities, fund infrastructure, or contract for off-site services; two, warehouse conversion may be faster and cheaper than building from scratch, which matters during capacity shortages; three, courts should not substitute local political preferences for agency expertise on detention needs.

Third, stronger detention capacity can improve immigration enforcement and public order. One, more beds reduce overcrowding and release pressure in the system; two, predictable detention capacity can speed removals and case processing; three, if the government cannot detain at scale, it may incentivize unlawful entry and undermine border policy credibility.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between local externalities and national enforcement capacity. Prop wins if the round prioritizes who bears the costs of policy implementation, while Opp wins if the round treats immigration detention as a core federal function that cannot be hostage to local vetoes.
motion_areas: TH, as the federal government, would prioritize building immigration detention facilities in rural communities over urban areas
THBT local governments should be able to block federal detention facilities on environmental grounds
THP a world where federal immigration enforcement facilities require local consent before construction

cards.title: US-Brokered Ceasefire Extension Buys Time But Risks Freezing the Israel-Hezbollah Conflict
cards.background: Israel and Lebanon agreed to a 45-day extension of their ceasefire after two days of talks in Washington, according to the US state department. The previous truce between Israel and Hezbollah was due to expire on Sunday, and further negotiations are scheduled for 2-3 June. On the same day, the Israeli military said it struck Hezbollah sites in southern Lebanon, while Lebanon’s health ministry said nearly 40 people were wounded near Tyre and that a primary healthcare centre was levelled and Hiram hospital was damaged, injuring six medical staff.

prop_args.thesis: Extending the ceasefire is the least-bad option because it prevents immediate escalation while creating diplomatic space for a more durable border settlement.
mechanisms: First, it reduces the risk of a rapid military spiral. This is because (1) the truce was about to expire, so any lapse would have created a high-risk window for retaliation, (2) both sides are still actively exchanging fire, as shown by Israeli strikes and reported launches/alerts on the same day, and (3) even a short extension lowers the probability of miscalculation turning into a broader war.

Second, it preserves US leverage over both parties. Three reasons: one, Washington is already hosting the talks, so the extension keeps the US at the center of the process; two, a time-bound extension forces continued negotiations rather than letting either side declare victory and walk away; three, the stated agenda of sovereignty, territorial integrity, and border security gives the US a concrete framework to push for implementation steps.

Third, it protects civilians and critical infrastructure in the short run. This matters because (1) the article shows direct harm to non-combatants, including nearly 40 wounded and six medical staff injured, (2) damage to a primary healthcare centre and hospital creates cascading humanitarian costs beyond the immediate strike, and (3) even temporary de-escalation can keep aid, medical access, and displacement levels from worsening further.

opp_args.thesis: A ceasefire extension without enforcement merely freezes the conflict, giving Hezbollah and Israel time to rearm, regroup, and continue low-level violence under diplomatic cover.
mechanisms: First, it entrenches a status quo of managed instability. One, the article shows the truce is already shaky and violations are ongoing; two, if neither side pays a cost for continued strikes, the extension becomes a permission structure for limited violence; three, this normalizes a border regime where periodic attacks replace real peace.

Second, it weakens incentives for a final settlement. One, time-bound extensions let both sides postpone hard concessions on sovereignty, territorial integrity, and border arrangements; two, each side can use the pause to improve its bargaining position militarily and politically; three, repeated extensions can become an endless holding pattern that avoids the core dispute.

Third, it can worsen humanitarian and political outcomes by prolonging uncertainty. One, civilians and hospitals remain exposed because the conflict is not actually resolved; two, repeated strikes during a nominal ceasefire undermine trust in diplomacy and make local populations less willing to support compromise; three, the longer the conflict drags on, the more likely it is that a single incident triggers a larger breakdown.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the extension is a genuine bridge to settlement or just a pause that institutionalizes low-level war. Prop wins if the round prioritizes immediate civilian protection and crisis prevention; opp wins if it shows that without enforcement and a political endgame, the extension simply delays a larger explosion.
motion_areas: TH, as the US, would broker short-term ceasefire extensions in active border conflicts
THBT temporary ceasefire extensions are preferable to allowing truces to expire when final peace is not yet possible
THP a world where ceasefires can be extended repeatedly without a final settlement

cards.title: Alberta Separatism Exposes the Limits of Canadian Federal Bargaining Over Oil and Climate
cards.background: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Alberta on Friday to announce a preliminary agreement on a crude oil pipeline with Premier Danielle Smith. The trip came days after a provincial court ruled that separatists had not followed proper procedure in collecting signatures for a referendum on Alberta secession, saying the process should have triggered consultation with Indigenous peoples whose treaty rights could be affected. One separatist group, Stay Free Alberta, said it had submitted more than 300,000 signatures, while polls have shown roughly one-third of Albertans support secession. The political backdrop includes Ottawa’s climate regulations, Alberta’s oil-and-gas economy, and tensions with the United States under President Donald Trump, including tariffs and reported separatist outreach to U.S. State Department officials.

prop_args.thesis: Ottawa should compromise more aggressively with Alberta on pipelines and resource policy because economic accommodation is the best way to neutralize separatist pressure and preserve the Canadian federation.
mechanisms: First, accommodation undercuts the core grievance driving separatism. This is because (1) Alberta’s separatist pitch is built around the claim that Ottawa over-regulates oil and gas, (2) visible policy wins like a pipeline and looser investment conditions give moderates a reason to stay inside Canada, and (3) when the federal government delivers material benefits, it splits the coalition between hard separatists and frustrated but persuadable voters.

Second, federal compromise reduces the risk of a self-reinforcing political escalation. Three reasons: one, if Ottawa is seen as dismissive, separatists can frame themselves as the only defenders of Alberta’s interests; two, a court setback does not eliminate the underlying anger, so symbolic confrontation can revive the movement; three, a negotiated settlement is cheaper than managing a long-term legitimacy crisis in a province that is economically central to Canada’s energy sector.

Third, stabilizing Alberta protects national economic output and bargaining power with the United States. This matters because (1) Alberta’s oil and gas sector is a major export engine, (2) federal-provincial unity strengthens Canada’s hand in tariff disputes with Trump-era U.S. pressure, and (3) uncertainty over secession or conflict over pipelines raises investment risk, delays infrastructure, and depresses long-run growth.

opp_args.thesis: Ottawa should resist separatist pressure and maintain stronger federal climate and constitutional constraints because conceding to Alberta rewards coercive regional politics and weakens national governance.
mechanisms: First, concessions create moral hazard for regional blackmail. One, if Alberta gets policy wins whenever separatism rises, other provinces learn that threatening exit is an effective bargaining tool; two, this incentivizes more radical provincial politics over time; three, the federal government loses the ability to set coherent national standards on climate, taxation, and infrastructure.

Second, weakening environmental rules for a pipeline locks Canada into high-carbon dependence and long-term policy costs. One, carbon-intensive infrastructure creates stranded-asset risk if global climate policy tightens; two, it makes it harder for Ottawa to meet emissions targets and maintain credibility with investors and allies; three, the short-term economic gain may be outweighed by higher transition costs later.

Third, the legal setback shows separatism is procedurally and constitutionally fragile, so Ottawa does not need to overreact. One, the court ruling already slowed the referendum path by requiring Indigenous consultation; two, the movement still lacks a clear majority, with support around one-third of the province; three, firm federalism can contain the issue without paying the political price of major concessions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether accommodation buys durable stability or simply rewards a veto threat. Prop wins if you prioritize immediate federation management and investment certainty; opp wins if you think conceding on pipelines and climate creates a long-term moral hazard that erodes national policy capacity.
motion_areas: TH, as the Canadian federal government, would make major policy concessions to Alberta to prevent separatism
THBT federal governments should prioritize territorial unity over environmental regulation in resource-rich regions
THP a world where subnational separatist movements can credibly force economic concessions from central governments

cards.title: Powell’s Exit Opens a Battle Over Whether the Fed Should Prioritize Inflation Discipline or Growth Support
cards.background: Jerome Powell’s term as Federal Reserve Chair ends on May 15, 2026, after a tenure shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent inflation surge. Bloomberg’s coverage frames the transition as a possible “regime change” at the Fed, with Kevin Warsh discussed as a potential successor and Lael Brainard commenting on the institution’s future. The key context is that the Fed has spent the past several years balancing high inflation, interest-rate hikes, and concerns about growth and financial stability.

prop_args.thesis: A more hawkish, credibility-focused Fed leadership is necessary to anchor inflation expectations and preserve long-run economic stability.
mechanisms: First, a tougher chair restores anti-inflation credibility. This is because (1) households and firms form wage and price expectations based on whether the Fed is willing to keep rates high, (2) after the post-pandemic inflation spike, any sign of softness risks re-embedding inflation into contracts and pricing behavior, and (3) a credible commitment to price stability lowers the risk premium investors demand on U.S. assets.

Second, regime change can reduce the chance of policy being too politically reactive. Three reasons: one, an independent Fed can absorb short-term pain that elected officials cannot, two, a chair willing to tolerate slower growth can prevent premature easing, and three, clearer anti-inflation signaling reduces the boom-bust cycle caused by stop-start monetary policy.

Third, the long-run welfare gain outweighs the short-run growth cost. This matters because inflation is a regressive tax that hits low-income households hardest through food, rent, and borrowing costs, so even if tighter policy slows hiring temporarily, it protects purchasing power and avoids a deeper later recession caused by unanchored inflation.

opp_args.thesis: A regime shift at the Fed risks over-tightening, politicizing monetary policy, and causing unnecessary damage to employment and financial stability.
mechanisms: First, a more hawkish chair can overshoot and engineer avoidable recession. One, monetary policy works with long and variable lags, two, the Fed can keep tightening after inflation has already peaked because the data arrives late, and three, that delay means rate hikes hit jobs, housing, and credit conditions after the economy has already cooled.

Second, changing leadership can undermine institutional continuity and market confidence. One, investors may read the transition as a break from the Powell-era consensus, two, uncertainty about the new chair’s reaction function increases volatility in bond and equity markets, and three, firms delay investment when they cannot predict the cost of capital.

Third, prioritizing inflation too narrowly ignores distributional and systemic risks. One, higher rates disproportionately crush mortgage borrowers, small businesses, and leveraged sectors, two, unemployment and bankruptcies create scarring that lasts beyond the inflation episode, and three, the Fed’s mandate is dual-purpose, so sacrificing labor-market health for symbolic toughness is economically inefficient.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the main threat is persistent inflation or policy-induced recession. Prop wins if you believe credibility is fragile and that the Fed must overcorrect to prevent a second inflation wave; opp wins if you think the post-pandemic inflation shock is already fading and the real danger is lagged monetary tightening causing avoidable damage.
motion_areas: TH, as the Federal Reserve, would prioritize inflation over unemployment even at the cost of a recession
THBT central banks should be more hawkish after an inflation shock
THP a world where the Fed is led by a more politically independent and anti-inflation chair
TH, as the United States, would appoint a more aggressive Fed Chair after a major inflation episode

cards.title: Aggressive War Remains Largely Unpunished as Nuremberg’s Promise Fades
cards.background: The article reviews Lawrence Douglas’s book The Criminal State and argues that international law has shifted away from prosecuting the crime of aggression since the 1946 Nuremberg trials. It notes that the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin for war crimes, but aggression charges remain effectively unavailable against non-party states such as the United States, Israel, and Russia. The piece also cites the 2010 criminal definition of aggression and argues that recent conflicts, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, show the limits of current enforcement.

prop_args.thesis: Reviving aggression prosecutions would restore deterrence against the most upstream cause of mass atrocities and make international law meaningfully constrain war-makers.
mechanisms: First, aggression prosecutions target the decision-makers who start wars, not just the battlefield excesses that follow. This is because (1) leaders can often frame atrocities as accidental or rogue behavior, (2) punishing only war crimes leaves the strategic choice to invade untouched, and (3) making initiation of war itself criminal raises the personal cost for presidents, generals, and cabinets who otherwise externalize the human cost onto civilians.

Second, a real aggression regime would strengthen deterrence by closing the current impunity gap. Three reasons: one, the article shows that the ICC can issue war-crimes warrants but not meaningful aggression charges against major powers; two, states currently calculate that they can invade first and litigate later; three, even symbolic legal exposure can constrain travel, coalition-building, asset access, and post-war legitimacy for elites.

Third, this improves the quality of post-conflict justice and prevention. This matters because (1) atrocity trials alone treat symptoms after mass death has already occurred, (2) aggression findings establish the causal chain from invasion to later crimes, and (3) that record helps victims, historians, and future courts identify responsibility earlier and more accurately.

opp_args.thesis: Aggression prosecutions are politically selective, legally vague, and likely to weaken international law by overpromising what cannot be enforced.
mechanisms: First, the crime of aggression is inherently contested and easy to weaponize politically. One, the article notes that states only agreed on a criminal definition in 2010 after decades of disagreement; two, self-defense and aggression are often disputed in real time; three, powerful states and their allies will always argue that their interventions were lawful, making prosecutions look like victor’s justice.

Second, the enforcement architecture is structurally incapable of reaching the most important targets. One, non-parties such as the United States, Israel, and Russia cannot be charged with aggression at the ICC; two, even member-state exemptions hollow out the rule; three, without universal jurisdiction or Security Council consensus, the regime mainly captures weaker states and leaves great powers untouched.

Third, focusing on aggression can crowd out the more achievable and valuable atrocity cases. One, war-crimes and crimes-against-humanity trials already generate victim testimony and historical record; two, they are more legible to courts because they focus on conduct rather than the legality of a war’s initiation; three, a failed aggression regime risks discrediting the broader project of international criminal justice.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic norm-setting and actual enforcement. Pro side wins if the question is whether international law should condemn war initiation in principle; opposition wins if the standard is whether a rule that cannot bind great powers will improve outcomes rather than simply create selective, politicized justice.

THBT the international community should create an ad hoc tribunal for aggression against Russia
THP a world where leaders can be held personally liable for starting wars
THBT international law should treat aggressive war as the primary international crime
TH, as developing states, would support expanding aggression jurisdiction at the ICC

cards.title: Trump’s Boeing Deal With China Looks More Like Summit Optics Than a Trade Breakthrough
cards.background: On 15 May 2026, US President Donald Trump said China had agreed to buy 200 Boeing jets, with the possibility of up to 750 planes if Boeing “does a good job.” Neither the Chinese government nor Boeing confirmed the deal, and key details such as aircraft type, delivery schedule, and whether the planes are new orders were not disclosed. Aviation intelligence firm IBA estimated the 200-plane package at about $17bn to $19bn if 80% are 737 MAX jets, or up to $25bn if a larger share are widebody aircraft. The announcement came during Trump’s trip to Beijing, where Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg joined other US executives seeking market access in China.

prop_args.thesis: Even an unconfirmed Boeing package is economically and politically meaningful because it signals a partial reopening of China’s market to US aerospace and gives both sides a face-saving off-ramp from trade escalation.
mechanisms: First, the deal restores commercial access to a strategically important market. This is because (1) China is one of the world’s largest aviation growth markets, (2) Boeing had been largely shut out amid US-China trade tensions, and (3) even a 200-plane order creates a pipeline for future maintenance, parts, and services revenue beyond the headline sale.

Second, the announcement improves bargaining leverage for both governments. Three reasons: one, Trump can present it as proof that tariffs and pressure yielded concrete gains; two, Beijing can use the purchase to buy time and reduce immediate trade friction without making a broad policy concession; three, the prospect of a larger 750-plane follow-on creates a credible incentive structure for continued engagement.

Third, the deal helps Boeing and GE Aerospace materially. This matters because Boeing shares had already fallen nearly 4 percent on Thursday and were still down about 2.6 percent on Friday, while GE Aerospace fell 2 percent; a large order book supports production planning, supplier confidence, and investor sentiment in a sector where scale and backlog are critical.

opp_args.thesis: This is mostly political theatre, not a durable economic breakthrough, because the announcement lacks confirmation, lacks detail, and is vulnerable to reversal or re-bundling.
mechanisms: First, the absence of formal confirmation makes the headline unreliable as a real trade gain. One, neither Boeing nor the Chinese government issued a confirming statement; two, planemakers usually disclose major deals only once formalised; three, China has previously bundled repeat announcements with diplomatic visits, so the same aircraft may be counted more than once.

Second, the deal does not solve the structural reasons Boeing has lost ground in China. One, Airbus has already pulled far ahead in the Chinese market; two, China’s homegrown COMAC C919 is intended to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers; three, concerns over after-sales support and US export restrictions on parts make Chinese buyers wary of long-term reliance on Boeing.

Third, the announcement may have limited macroeconomic impact. One, Trump’s broader tariff strategy has not significantly reduced the US trade deficit; two, the trade truce still expires in five months and was not extended; three, without follow-on purchases in agriculture and energy, the summit remains heavy on atmospherics and light on substance.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between a symbolic headline and a durable commercial shift. Prop wins if the question is whether the announcement creates real leverage and market confidence; opp wins if the standard is whether this is a confirmed, structurally meaningful breakthrough, because the deal is unverified, potentially recycled, and does not resolve Boeing’s deeper competitive disadvantages in China.

THBT summit diplomacy is a more effective tool than broad tariffs for managing US-China economic competition

cards.title: Russian Mass Aerial Strikes Push Ukraine Toward Escalatory Deep-Strike Strategy
cards.background: On Thursday, Russia launched what Ukraine described as its largest aerial assault since the war began more than four years ago, striking a nine-storey apartment block in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district and killing at least 24 people, including three children. In response, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said strikes on Russia’s oil industry and military production facilities were “entirely justified” and said he had discussed long-range strikes with senior military, security and intelligence officials. Ukraine then launched a large-scale drone attack on Friday against energy and military infrastructure across several Russian regions, including a strike on the Ryazan oil refinery that killed at least four people, including a child. The escalation came alongside a 205-for-205 prisoner swap and the exchange of 526 Russian bodies for 41 Ukrainian bodies, following a three-day ceasefire brokered by US President Donald Trump.

prop_args.thesis: Ukraine is rationally escalating deep strikes because only by imposing direct costs on Russia’s war economy can it deter further mass bombardment and improve its bargaining position.
mechanisms: First, deep strikes target the material base of Russia’s war machine. This is because (1) oil refineries, military production sites, and logistics nodes are the inputs that sustain missile production, drone operations, and sustained air campaigns; (2) hitting these assets forces Russia to divert air defenses, repair capacity, and budget away from the front; and (3) repeated damage compounds over time, making each new strike more expensive to absorb than the last.

Second, escalation creates deterrence by punishment. Three reasons: one, Russia has shown it is willing to absorb diplomatic costs for civilian strikes, so only military/economic pain changes incentives; two, striking inside Russia raises the domestic political cost for the Kremlin by showing the war is no longer geographically contained; three, it signals that attacks on Kyiv will trigger asymmetric retaliation rather than one-sided victimhood.

Third, this improves Ukraine’s leverage in any ceasefire or peace process. This matters because (1) Trump’s own comments suggest battlefield shocks can delay or shape peace efforts; (2) if Russia’s energy and military infrastructure becomes vulnerable, Moscow has stronger reasons to accept limits on strikes; and (3) Ukraine needs to demonstrate it can impose costs even without matching Russia’s scale in conventional firepower.

opp_args.thesis: Deep-strike escalation is strategically self-defeating because it invites retaliation, hardens Russian resolve, and reduces the chances of a negotiated settlement.
mechanisms: First, escalation can trigger a spiral that harms Ukraine more than Russia. One, Russia has already shown willingness to conduct the largest aerial assault of the war, so it can respond with even more intense strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure; two, Ukraine’s limited air defense capacity means each Russian retaliation has a higher marginal effect on civilian casualties; three, the conflict becomes less controllable once both sides normalize attacks on rear-area economic targets.

Second, strikes on Russian territory can strengthen Kremlin propaganda and mobilization. One, Moscow can frame them as proof that Ukraine is an aggressor rather than a victim, helping justify further conscription, repression, and war spending; two, civilian casualties in places like Ryazan create domestic outrage that reduces pressure on Putin to compromise; three, the Russian state can use the attacks to rally nationalist support around a defensive war narrative.

Third, this undermines diplomacy at the exact moment limited progress exists. One, the 205-for-205 prisoner swap and body exchange show that transactional de-escalation channels still exist; two, Trump’s ceasefire-brokered process is fragile and can be derailed by headline-grabbing strikes; three, if the goal is a ceasefire, signaling willingness to hit Russian oil infrastructure makes Moscow less likely to trust or accept future terms.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercive escalation actually changes Russian behavior faster than it provokes counter-escalation. Prop wins if the round is about stopping an ongoing war economy, because Ukraine cannot outgun Russia conventionally and therefore needs asymmetric leverage; Opp wins if the round prioritizes civilian protection and peace prospects, because each escalation cycle can produce immediate civilian costs before any strategic gains materialize.
motion_areas: TH, as Ukraine, would prioritize deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure
THBT states under invasion should escalate attacks on the aggressor’s war economy
THP a world where Ukraine is given unrestricted long-range strike capability
THBT peace negotiations should not constrain a defending state’s ability to retaliate

cards.title: US Capital Punishment in a Terror Case Hardens the Domestic Response to Anti-Israel Political Violence
cards.background: The US Department of Justice said on 15 May 2026 that it will seek the death penalty for Elias Rodriguez, 31, who is charged with killing two Israeli embassy staff members outside the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington DC in May 2025. Prosecutors say Rodriguez fired 20 shots at Yaron Lischinsky, 30, and Sarah Lynn Milgrim, 26, after traveling from Chicago to Washington with a handgun and researching a networking event for young Jewish professionals. He faces 13 charges, including murder of a foreign official, hate crimes, and acts of terrorism; he has pleaded not guilty. The move comes after President Donald Trump restored and expanded federal death-penalty policy, reversing Joe Biden’s moratorium on federal executions.

prop_args.thesis: Seeking the death penalty is the strongest available signal that the state will treat politically motivated anti-Semitic violence as terrorism, not protest, and will deter copycat attacks.
mechanisms: First, it reclassifies the act in the public mind from a politically charged homicide into a high-salience terror offense. This is because (1) the target was foreign diplomatic staff, (2) the attack was allegedly premeditated with online research and a manifesto, and (3) the maximum punishment communicates that the state sees this as an assault on the political order, not a spontaneous crime.

Second, it increases deterrence for would-be extremists who are motivated by notoriety and ideological validation. Three reasons: one, the death penalty raises the personal cost of carrying out a symbolic attack; two, it reduces the chance that attackers view prison as a platform for radicalization and martyrdom; three, it signals to online networks that the US will not normalize violence wrapped in political language.

Third, it reassures vulnerable communities and foreign diplomats that the US will defend them with the full force of the law. This matters because (1) Jewish communities and embassy personnel are likely to feel more protected, (2) allied states read leniency as weakness in protecting diplomats, and (3) a firm response preserves the credibility of US commitments to counterterrorism and diplomatic security.

opp_args.thesis: Seeking death in a politically charged case is counterproductive because it turns the defendant into a martyr, deepens polarization, and does little to improve security.
mechanisms: First, it can amplify extremist narratives and create a martyrdom effect. One, the suspect already framed the attack in ideological terms; two, a capital case gives propaganda value to supporters who portray him as being killed for his politics; three, the long appeals process keeps the case in the public eye and sustains radical attention.

Second, it risks normalizing the death penalty as a tool for symbolic politics rather than narrow public safety. One, once the state uses capital punishment in a highly salient terror case, future administrations can expand it to more categories; two, it lowers the threshold for politically motivated executions; three, it undermines the moral distinction between justice and revenge.

Third, it may worsen domestic and international backlash without addressing root causes. One, Jewish communities may face retaliatory hate if the case inflames tensions; two, Palestinians and pro-Palestinian activists may see the prosecution as proof of selective justice, increasing alienation; three, the policy does nothing to reduce online radicalization, hate speech, or access to weapons.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic deterrence and symbolic escalation. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes state credibility and protection of vulnerable targets; opp wins if they think the death penalty mainly feeds martyrdom and polarization while adding little marginal security.
motion_areas: TH, as the US government, would seek the death penalty for ideologically motivated terrorist murderers
THBT states should abolish the federal death penalty even for terrorism cases
THP a world where governments prioritize life imprisonment over capital punishment for political violence

cards.title: Russia Can Exploit NATO’s Decision Lag to Sever the Baltics Before Article 5 Bites
cards.background: The article reports on a December 2025 war game at Germany’s Helmut Schmidt University in Hamburg, where the author played the Russian chief of general staff and won by attacking Lithuania. The scenario assumed a hypothetical Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in summer 2026, after which Russia could redeploy experienced forces from the Ukraine war and threaten NATO’s eastern flank. The Red Team used roughly 100,000 Russian troops in the wider theater, including about 12,000 forward troops from Belarus and additional forces from Kaliningrad, to cut the Suwalki Gap and isolate the Baltics from Poland and the rest of NATO.

prop_args.thesis: Russia’s post-Ukraine force regeneration and NATO’s slow reinforcement cycle create a real window in which Moscow can coerce or sever the Baltics before the alliance can respond effectively.
mechanisms: First, Russia can mass faster than NATO in the opening phase. This is because (1) Russian troops and equipment can already be pre-positioned in Belarus and Kaliningrad, (2) NATO needs days to weeks to move reinforcements into the theater, and (3) a limited offensive can seize key terrain before a counterattack is organized.

Second, Russia can convert a small incursion into strategic paralysis. Three reasons: one, cutting the Suwalki Gap isolates Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia from overland NATO support; two, hybrid cover and exercises let Russia hide mobilization until the last moment; three, once the corridor is fortified, NATO faces a much harder and bloodier retaking operation.

Third, Russian escalation dominance deters NATO from reversing the fait accompli. This matters because (1) Moscow can threaten tactical nuclear use from Belarus, Kaliningrad, or western Russia, (2) Germany and other European states may not be willing to risk direct war without U.S. backing, and (3) if Washington stays out for 48 hours, European resolve is likely to fracture before Article 5 becomes operationally meaningful.

opp_args.thesis: The war game overstates Russian advantage because a real attack on the Baltics would trigger faster allied adaptation, stronger political unity, and severe Russian escalation costs.
mechanisms: First, NATO is not a static target. One, intelligence and surveillance would likely detect Russian buildup earlier than the game assumes; two, forward-deployed allied forces, air policing, and rapid U.S. reinforcement could blunt the initial thrust; three, once the attack is unmistakable, Article 5 creates strong pressure for collective response rather than German unilateral hesitation.

Second, Russia’s operation is far more fragile than the scenario suggests. One, the terrain in Lithuania is narrow, forested, and swampy, which favors defenders and ambushes; two, the forward force is only about 12,000 troops on the main axis, making it vulnerable to attrition; three, if the incursion stalls, Russia risks losing the political shock effect that the whole plan depends on.

Third, nuclear brinkmanship is not costless and may backfire. One, threatening tactical nuclear use could unify NATO and justify U.S. intervention; two, it would intensify sanctions and isolate Russia diplomatically; three, European states may conclude that yielding once only invites more coercion, so they may choose escalation now to avoid a worse precedent later.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between military capability and political willingness: the article’s core claim is not that Russia can win a long war, but that it can win the first 48 hours by exploiting allied hesitation. Prop wins if the judge believes decision lag and nuclear fear matter more than battlefield attrition; opp wins if they show NATO can absorb the shock, mobilize faster, and treat any Baltic incursion as a credibility test too costly to lose.
motion_areas: TH, as NATO, would pre-commit to automatic military retaliation against any incursion into the Baltics
THBT Europe should prioritize rapid-reaction conventional forces over nuclear deterrence in defending the eastern flank
THP a world where the U.S. reduces its security guarantee to Europe
THBT Germany should adopt a more explicit war-fighting posture toward Russia
TH, as the EU, would station permanent combat brigades in the Baltics

About 12,000 ground troops formed the forward advance force from Belarus

The operation aimed to cut the Suwalki Gap and link Kaliningrad with Belarus within 24 hours
NATO’s European response was modeled as delayed by days to weeks, with the U.S. staying out for at least 48 hours

cards.title: Trump’s China Reset Buys Trade Optics While Deferring Taiwan and Iran Escalation
cards.background: US President Donald Trump completed a three-day visit to China, his first trip there in his second term, and said the talks produced broad trade deals but little clarity on Taiwan or Iran. Trump said he discussed Taiwan with Xi Jinping but made no commitment on the island’s status, and he also said he was still deciding whether to approve a major new US weapons package for Taipei. On Iran, Trump said he and Xi discussed the US-Israeli war and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, while Chinese officials said only that disputes should be resolved through negotiations. Trump also claimed China agreed to buy 200 Boeing jets and may increase purchases of US oil and farm goods, though neither side released detailed agreements and Beijing’s official recap did not mention new deals.

prop_args.thesis: A transactional US-China thaw can reduce immediate escalation risks by keeping Taiwan and Iran in managed ambiguity while preserving channels for trade and crisis communication.
mechanisms: First, the visit creates a face-saving off-ramp for both sides on Taiwan. This is because (1) Trump explicitly made no commitment either way on Taiwan, (2) Xi got a public reiteration that the US is not endorsing Taiwanese independence, and (3) ambiguity lowers the chance that either side feels forced into a maximalist response in the short term.

Second, trade engagement gives both governments incentives to avoid confrontation. Three reasons: one, China’s reported interest in Boeing jets, oil, and farm goods ties economic cooperation to stability; two, the US delegation of business leaders signals that commercial gains are politically valuable; three, both sides can point to “success” domestically, which reduces pressure to escalate on security issues to prove toughness.

Third, keeping Iran discussions within diplomacy rather than coercion can help reopen the Strait of Hormuz and reduce spillover into a wider regional war. This matters because (1) China has leverage with Tehran and can act as a channel, (2) both Washington and Beijing publicly endorsed negotiations, and (3) even limited coordination on shipping lanes lowers global energy shock risk.

opp_args.thesis: The summit mainly exposes strategic drift: vague trade promises do not solve the underlying security conflict, and ambiguity on Taiwan and Iran increases the risk of miscalculation later.
mechanisms: First, the lack of concrete commitments on Taiwan makes deterrence less credible. One, Trump said he had not decided on the weapons package, which signals hesitation to Beijing; two, China can read this as an opening to pressure Taipei more aggressively; three, Taiwan is left uncertain about US resolve, which weakens allied confidence and invites brinkmanship.

Second, the Iran discussion is too shallow to change battlefield realities. One, Trump said he was not 'asking for any favors,' so China has no binding role in enforcement; two, Chinese officials only repeated generic support for negotiations, showing no shift in leverage over Tehran; three, without concrete coordination, the Strait of Hormuz remains vulnerable and the war can still widen through shipping disruption or proxy escalation.

Third, the trade announcements may be mostly optics and therefore create false confidence. One, no detailed agreements were released, so the supposed deals may not materialize; two, China’s official statement omitted new purchases, suggesting divergence between rhetoric and reality; three, if the summit is sold as a success without substance, both sides may delay harder decisions until the next crisis, when bargaining space is smaller.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether ambiguity is stabilizing or merely postpones confrontation. Prop wins if you prioritize immediate crisis management and the value of keeping both sides talking; opp wins if you think deterrence and credibility matter more than short-term optics, because unresolved Taiwan and Iran flashpoints remain live and can escalate fast.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize trade détente with China over immediate confrontation on Taiwan
THBT the US should seek Chinese cooperation on Iran even at the cost of softening pressure on Beijing over Taiwan
THP a world where major powers use economic deals to manage security disputes
THBT strategic ambiguity is preferable to explicit commitments in US-China relations
